I first heard of the historian Cho-yun Hsu through an interview with him by the writer and TV interviewer Xu Zhiyuan, and came away deeply impressed by his learning. Last year I happened to see this book at a Sisyphe bookstore in Beijing (a Chinese bookstore chain) and bought it online (online it costs less than half the Sisyphe price, after all).

After more than ten years in Europe, I’ve become very interested in the characters of different nations and peoples, and in their stereotypes, and I had the idea of looking to history for the reasons. So I bought Why the Germans Do It Better and this book, hoping to discover what makes Germans German and the Chinese Chinese. I gave up on the first one before finishing it; the writing wasn’t very engaging. This one I’ve just finished, so while it’s still fresh, here are a few ideas I found interesting.

  • The north–south divide. The north was ruled by the Liao, Jin and Yuan for several hundred years, so the differences between northern and southern China today are really a continuation from centuries ago, even though the Ming and Qing reunified the country in between.
  • Valuing the civil over the military began with the Song dynasty.
  • A unified China is not the historical norm. The Song never unified the whole realm; history textbooks simply treat the Song as the legitimate heir of Chinese civilization and say little about the other states on what is now Chinese territory (the Western Xia, Liao, Jin, Tibet and so on).
  • Unlike Arab countries, or other Western countries with a single religion, China has had Buddhism, Confucianism and Taoism side by side. Is that why so many people have no faith today?
  • Many writers have lamented, with regret and resignation, the cultural shackles in place since the Ming dynasty, and Professor Hsu is no exception. Starting with the eight-legged essay, the rigid format of the imperial civil-service exams, Chinese thought was shackled. The century after the Opium Wars brought every kind of clash between Chinese and Western ideas and saw new ideas emerge, yet even today we still seem to be living in some continuation of the Ming and Qing. Clearly, what history passes down need not be continuous in time.
  • “The setbacks and humiliations China has suffered internationally since the nineteenth century have produced in the Chinese a complex of inferiority and false pride.” I strongly agree with this line. This conflicted personality is somewhat like the Germans’: the shame that followed World War II combined with a great power’s sense of superiority, which together have shaped the character of several generations of Germans. As I recall, Why the Germans Do It Better makes a similar point.
